name: redteam
arm: P1 of docs/research/preregistration.md, proposed and not registered: this result is an engineering check of card X14, no arm's result, and enters no registered analysis
wording: what the content guards and the trust floors stop, and what they wrongly stop, on this corpus: a deterministic measurement with no model in the loop, never a claim of defence
not_run: medium+secrets-block and medium+all (card E2.9's guards): not enforced on this commit, which core's loader refuses; they join when E2.9 merges
medium+trust (card E2.11's unattested_floor and protect_trusted): not enforced on this commit, which core's loader refuses
limits: Small: AMSB has 15 attacks, so its per-family rates rest on one to four scenarios; the payload sets add 1,263 attack rows, but from two sources only.

Optimistic: AMSB comes from the same OWASP project whose detector patterns the injection screen copies (card E2.10), and card X14's controls were written by its author; the controls are not a sample of real memory.
Not a defence: every rule here is a regular expression or a source rule, and a careful attacker writes around it; the screen's own limits are in research/results/h1-injection-screen.json.
English-centred: the screen's patterns are English, and deepset's rows include German, so a row in another language passes them unread.
Model-free: survival is AMSB's rule, the canary coming back in a later read; whether a model would act on what came back is not measured (a live sub-arm would be its own proposal).
AMSB's protected-key family has no counterpart in Engram, which has no protected keys: a value such as superadmin is ordinary content, stopped only by a source rule.
Rates per source kind are not independent: the same entries are planted once per setting, route and kind, so the cells share their items and are never pooled into one interval.
